{{Infobox person|birth_date=1295|death_date=1364|birth_place=[[Suwa District, Nagano]]|gender=[[Male (gender)]]|nationality=[[Japan]]|family=[[Suwa clan]]|notable_works=[[Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba]]}}
'''Enchū Suwa/Kosaka Enchū''' (諏訪 円忠/小坂 円忠) ([[Einin]] 3 ([[1295]]) – [[Jōji]] 3 ([[1364]])) was an official of the [[Kamakura shogunate]] and [[Ashikaga shogunate]], and the founder of the [[Suwa clan|Kyoto Suwa clan]]. He is the author of the [[Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba]].

== Life ==

Born in [[Shinano Province]], Suwa District, Enchū was the son of Suwa Moritada. According to the [[Kami Clan Genealogy]], he was a branch member of the [[Suwa-taisha]] Upper Shrine family and inherited the position of [[Jitō|jitō]] for [[Shinomiya-shō]] Funayama village in [[Hanishina District, Nagano|Hanishina District]], leading to his alternate name, '''Kosaka Enchū'''. His holdings also included lands in [[Etchū Province]], Takagi Village, and the villages of Miyake-gō Jūniri and Akanoi in [[Ōmi Province]]. The Suwa clan served as [[hikan]] under the [[Hōjō clan]], and Enchū’s uncle Suwa Tokimitsu was also an official of the Kamakura shogunate, fostering Enchū’s upbringing and service in Kamakura.

After the fall of the Hōjō clan, Enchū traveled to Kyoto and, through the mediation of [[Musō Soseki]], entered the service of [[Ashikaga Takauji]]. He rose through the Ranks from [[Hyōjōshū]] to protectorate administrator, eventually overseeing the construction of [[Tenryū-ji]]. He later became the administrator of [[Sōroku]], managing Zen-related issues. Enchū also contributed to the revival of the Suwa clan, whose main line had declined after the [[Nakasendai Rebellion]], and helped establish a system where warriors across Shinano participated in the annual Suwa Upper Shrine festival.

In [[Enbun]] 1 ([[1356]]), Enchū completed the [[Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba]], which bore a postscript by Takauji. This work spread Suwa faith throughout various strata of society, including the court nobility. As part of Takauji’s initiative to establish a national network of [[Ankoku-ji|Ankokuji temples]], Enchū founded [[Ankokoji (Chino City)]] near the Suwa Upper Shrine with Musō Soseki as its founding abbot.

Enchū also inherited knowledge of [[Falconry]] from the [[Q11536451]], a branch of the Suwa clan, as recorded in the [[Kami Clan Genealogy]]. This expertise was passed down among the heads of the Kyoto Suwa clan, and in [[Civilization|Bunmei]] 5 ([[1473]]), Suwa Tadakuni collaborated with the [[Asukai family|Asukai clan]] on annotated falconry waka poetry for [[Ashikaga Yoshimasa]], recorded in the [[Taka Hyakushu-chū]]. Tadakuni’s son, Suwa Sadamichi, compiled a treatise on falconry titled [[Taka Kikigaki Shōshō]].

Enchū also excelled in waka and renga poetry, with works selected for the [[Shinsenzai Wakashū|Shin Chokusenshū]], [[Shingoshūi Wakashū|Shin Goshūishū]], and [[Tsukubashū]].<ref>[https://www.ro-da.jp/shinshu-dcommons/museum_history/03OD0624101600] "Kami Clan Genealogy: Copy of Maeda Manuscript"</ref>
